options.C: Checking professional licensing with the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.D: Submitting proof of membership in an international union

explanation: Legal practice requires validating active licensure with the national regulatory body prior to clinical deployment. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of the orientation phase for new nursing staff?

options.A: Selecting candidates from an applicant pool
options.B: Assessing long-term retirement savings plans
options.C: Conducting annual performance salary reviews
options.D: Introducing hospital policies, safety protocols, and physical layout

explanation: Orientation acquaints the newly hired nurse with the immediate working environment and administrative rules. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h4)

question: How does effective onboarding benefit a healthcare organization?

options.A: It guarantees zero absenteeism across all nursing shifts
options.B: It completely replaces the need for continuing education
options.C: It reduces early employment anxiety and decreases turnover rates
options.D: It shifts all regulatory licensing duties to the employee

explanation: Proper integration helps new staff feel supported, lowering the likelihood of early resignation. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is a major consequence of maintaining unsafe patient-to-nurse ratios due to staffing shortages?

options.A: Elimination of the need for shift handovers
options.B: Faster patient discharge across all clinical units
options.C: Increased risk of nurse burnout and medication errors
options.D: Immediate reduction in hospital utility bills

explanation: High workloads and fatigue impair cognitive function, leading to a higher incidence of clinical mistakes. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h5)

question: When designing a unit shift roster, what key elements must nurse managers balance?

options.A: Hospital architectural design and pharmacy inventory
options.B: External regulatory audits and community outreach
options.C: Continuous coverage, skill mix, and staff fatigue prevention
options.D: Patient financial insurance status and physician schedules

explanation: Good rostering requires keeping the unit staffed with the right mix of skills while protecting staff from exhaustion. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is the primary focus of competency assessment in nursing?

options.A: Reviewing building maintenance and equipment purchase logs
options.B: Inspecting hospital sanitation and waste management
options.C: Calculating the monthly payroll and tax deductions
options.D: Verifying clinical skills, critical thinking, and procedural proficiency

explanation: Competency assessment specifically targets the practical skills and clinical judgment required for safe practice. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why are regular performance appraisals important for professional development?

options.A: They replace the need for professional licensing examinations
options.B: They determine the exact number of patients admitted daily
options.C: They provide documented feedback and identify educational gaps
options.D: They serve as the sole legal requirement for opening a private clinic

explanation: Appraisals highlight areas where a nurse excels and areas that require further training or mentorship. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is a direct result of healthcare institutions failing to invest in staff retention and development?

options.A: Complete elimination of patient complaints across wards
options.B: Experienced personnel migrating to better environments, causing brain drain
options.C: Automatic renewal of institutional licenses
options.D: Immediate improvement in hospital financial profitability

explanation: Lack of growth opportunities and poor retention incentives drive skilled workers away in search of better conditions. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h7)

question: How do continuing education programs contribute to healthcare quality?

options.A: They shorten the required duration of basic nursing training programs
options.B: They ensure that clinical knowledge and practices remain current and evidence-based
options.C: They reduce the cost of procuring specialized medical equipment
options.D: They eliminate the need for supervisory nursing staff on duty

explanation: Ongoing education updates the workforce on modern healthcare practices and new clinical guidelines. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is a legal consequence of knowingly assigning unqualified personnel to high-risk clinical areas?

options.A: Exemption from annual regulatory inspections
options.B: Reduction in patient length of stay
options.C: Exposure of the institution and manager to malpractice liability
options.D: Immediate promotion of the nursing director

explanation: Placing unqualified staff in roles beyond their competency breaches the standard of care and invites legal action. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h8)

question: What does the term 'moral injury' refer to in the context of chronic understaffing?

options.A: The financial penalty imposed by regulatory councils for missed shifts
options.B: The physical exhaustion caused by lifting heavy patients without assistance
options.C: The psychological distress experienced when unable to provide optimal care due to constraints
options.D: The legal dispute between hospital management and trade unions

explanation: Moral injury occurs when nurses are constrained from upholding their professional and ethical standards due to system failures. [learn more](GST321_U1_T11#GST321_U1_T11_h8)

question: What primary purpose do interdepartmental relationships serve in a hospital setting?

options.A: Ensuring seamless patient care flow between distinct hospital units
options.B: Eliminating the need for hierarchical nursing structures
options.C: Reducing the overall hospital budget for medical supplies
options.D: Standardizing the clinical nursing curriculum nationwide

explanation: Interdepartmental relationships connect various hospital units so that patient care transitions smoothly across departments. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why must nurse managers look beyond rigid departmental boundaries?

options.A: To prevent departments from sharing vital clinical equipment
options.B: To take over the administrative duties of pharmacy personnel
options.C: To foster a collaborative culture where shared goals supersede silos
options.D: To decrease the total number of hospital support services

explanation: Moving past rigid boundaries allows departments to work together effectively rather than operating in isolation. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h1)

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the SBAR communication framework?

options.A: Behavior
options.B: Background
options.C: Baseline
options.D: Bedside

explanation: In the SBAR tool, B represents Background, providing the contextual clinical history necessary for safe communication. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which practice best exemplifies closed-loop communication during an interdepartmental patient transfer?

options.A: Documenting the transfer only after the patient has been discharged home
options.B: The receiving nurse repeating the critical orders back to the sending nurse
options.C: Filling out the physical case note without speaking to the receiving unit
options.D: Sending a text message and assuming the receiving ward read it

explanation: Closed-loop communication requires the receiver to verify the message by repeating it back, ensuring total clarity. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which factor represents a structural barrier to interdepartmental communication?

options.A: Incompatible communication technologies and physical distance
options.B: Regular multidisciplinary clinical meetings
options.C: Excessive use of closed-loop communication techniques
options.D: Frequent utilization of the SBAR handover tool

explanation: Physical separation and poor technology infrastructure hinder timely information exchange between hospital units. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h3)

question: How do steep hierarchical gradients negatively impact interdepartmental collaboration?

options.A: They eliminate all forms of professional jargon between different departments.
options.B: They prevent junior staff from reporting vital safety issues due to intimidation.
options.C: They automatically resolve conflicts before management can intervene.
options.D: They encourage junior staff to take on senior administrative roles too quickly.

explanation: When power dynamics are intimidating, staff lower in the hierarchy may withhold critical observations out of fear. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h3)

question: What is the primary benefit of cross-departmental shadowing programs for nursing staff?

options.A: Allowing nurses to permanently change their assigned department
options.B: Fostering empathy and understanding of operational pressures in other units
options.C: Eliminating the need for formal hospital orientation programs
options.D: Reducing the total number of hospital administrative personnel

explanation: Shadowing allows nurses to experience daily realities in units like pharmacy or labs, improving mutual respect and teamwork. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h4)

question: Which management strategy encourages departments to view success collectively rather than competitively?

options.A: Enforcing strict departmental segregation
options.B: Establishing shared key performance indicators
options.C: Using complex medical jargon during handovers
options.D: Reducing the frequency of inter-unit meetings

explanation: Shared KPIs align goals across different units, promoting collaborative success over departmental rivalry. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is a common trigger for interdepartmental conflict in busy hospital settings?

options.A: Excessive use of standardized SBAR handovers
options.B: Resource scarcity and conflicting unit priorities
options.C: Too many cross-departmental shadowing programs
options.D: Complete alignment of departmental goals

explanation: Competing for limited hospital resources and having differing operational priorities frequently spark inter-unit conflict. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h5)

question: When resolving a dispute between the ward and the laboratory, what should be the primary managerial focus?

options.A: Permanently separating the two conflicting departments
options.B: Ignoring the issue until staff resolve it independently
options.C: Collaborative problem-solving and analyzing process bottlenecks
options.D: Punishing the staff members who initiated the disagreement

explanation: Effective conflict resolution targets systemic process issues rather than assigning personal blame. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h5)

question: A patient experiences a delayed medication administration because the pharmacy and the nursing ward failed to communicate an out-of-stock notice. Which concept does this scenario best illustrate?

options.A: The positive outcome of eliminating hospital hierarchical gradients
options.B: The direct negative impact of poor interdepartmental relations on patient care
options.C: The effectiveness of shared departmental performance indicators
options.D: The success of closed-loop communication in emergency nursing

explanation: A breakdown in communication between nursing and pharmacy directly compromises timely patient treatment. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical outcome of robust interdepartmental collaboration in a hospital?

options.A: Improved patient satisfaction scores
options.B: Reduced hospital readmission rates
options.C: Decreased frequency of missed medication doses
options.D: Higher rates of preventable adverse clinical events

explanation: Robust collaboration reduces adverse events rather than increasing them; therefore, higher adverse event rates are incorrect. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which tool provides quantitative data regarding communication failures between hospital units?

options.A: Incident report tracking
options.B: Informal hallway conversations
options.C: Cross-departmental shadowing
options.D: Staff climate surveys

explanation: Incident reports supply measurable, quantitative data on errors resulting from communication breakdowns. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h7)

question: Why is it important for nursing administration to evaluate interdepartmental communication performance regularly?

options.A: To reduce the number of patient admissions in surgical wards
options.B: To transform subjective impressions of teamwork into actionable improvement data
options.C: To eliminate the need for future staff meetings and evaluations
options.D: To ensure that all departments adopt the exact same clinical procedures

explanation: Regular evaluation turns observations about teamwork into concrete metrics that guide quality improvement efforts. [learn more](GST321_U1_T12#GST321_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of the directing function in nursing management?

options.A: Putting operational plans into motion and guiding staff
options.B: Drafting hospital policies and legal compliance frameworks
options.C: Allocating financial budgets for the upcoming fiscal year
options.D: Conducting retrospective audits of patient health records

explanation: Directing focuses on execution, translating plans and organizational goals into active daily tasks and guiding personnel toward them. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h1)

question: How does directing differ from planning and organizing in a healthcare setting?

options.A: Planning deals with physical equipment, while directing handles monetary budgets exclusively.
options.B: Directing is a theoretical exercise, while planning requires direct patient care delivery.
options.C: Organizing is executed at the bedside, whereas directing occurs solely in administrative boardrooms.
options.D: Planning sets the objectives, whereas directing actively guides and oversees staff execution.

explanation: Planning and organizing establish the structure and framework, while directing provides the interpersonal drive and oversight to execute the work. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h1)

question: What principle of directing dictates that a staff nurse should receive instructions from only one designated supervisor?

options.A: Maximum individual contribution
options.B: Appropriate leadership technique
options.C: Harmony of objectives
options.D: Unity of command

explanation: Unity of command prevents role confusion and conflicting directives by ensuring subordinates report to and receive orders from a single superior. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h2)

question: Why is the principle of harmony of objectives critical in a busy hospital ward?

options.A: It ensures that doctors and nurses always work separate shifts without overlapping.
options.B: It eliminates the need for written nursing care plans during accreditation visits.
options.C: It legally binds the hospital to pay overtime for all emergency shifts worked.
options.D: It aligns personal career goals with institutional targets to reduce turnover and boost morale.

explanation: When personal and organizational goals are in harmony, staff members feel valued and are more motivated to achieve institutional targets. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h2)

question: Which leadership style is characterized by the manager making all decisions unilaterally without staff input?

options.A: Laissez-faire
options.B: Democratic
options.C: Autocratic
options.D: Transformational

explanation: An autocratic leader retains total authority, making decisions independently and issuing direct orders to subordinates. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h3)

question: A sudden mass casualty incident arrives at the accident and emergency unit. Which leadership style is most appropriate for the nurse manager to adopt initially?

options.A: Democratic
options.B: Autocratic
options.C: Laissez-faire
options.D: Participative

explanation: In high-stress, rapid-response emergencies, an autocratic style ensures quick, unambiguous direction and organized action. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h3)

question: What type of communication barrier is represented by the use of ambiguous medical jargon or confusing abbreviations?

options.A: Hierarchical barrier
options.B: Psychological barrier
options.C: Semantic barrier
options.D: Environmental barrier

explanation: Semantic barriers occur when words, acronyms, or symbols have different meanings to the sender and receiver, leading to misinterpretation. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h4)

question: Which of the following is an example of upward communication in a hospital ward?

options.A: The director of nursing issuing a new policy memo regarding mandatory uniform standards

options.C: A senior nurse discussing patient care management strategies with another senior nurse

question: According to Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which of the following is classified as a hygiene factor?

options.A: Opportunities for career advancement
options.B: Public recognition for clinical excellence
options.C: Working conditions and job security
options.D: Personal growth and increased responsibility

question: Why must nurse managers address basic physiological and safety needs before expecting nurses to engage in innovative quality improvement projects?

options.A: Lower-level survival needs must be satisfied before higher-level motivational needs become influential.
options.B: Hospital accreditation bodies legally forbid junior staff from joining committees.
options.C: Experienced nurses automatically reject any task that is not directly tied to bedside care.
options.D: Higher-level needs are irrelevant to healthcare professionals working in clinical units.

explanation: Based on Maslow's hierarchy, individuals are primarily driven by unmet basic needs like safety and security before they seek esteem or self-actualization. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h5)

question: What does the registered nurse retain when delegating a task to a qualified nursing assistant?

options.B: Exemption from all legal liability if harm occurs
options.C: Ultimate accountability for the patient outcome
options.D: Direct ownership of the assistant's professional license

question: Which criterion of the Five Rights of Delegation is being applied when a nurse assesses whether a patient is clinically stable before assigning a task?

options.A: Right circumstances
options.B: Right supervision
options.C: Right person
options.D: Right direction

question: Which conflict resolution strategy results in a win-win solution by fully satisfying the concerns of all parties involved?

options.A: Compromising
options.B: Smoothing
options.C: Avoiding
options.D: Collaborating

question: Two senior staff nurses argue frequently over scheduling preferences, creating a toxic ward environment. The manager brings them together to identify core needs and formulate a shared roster that satisfies both parties. What conflict strategy is this?

options.A: Avoiding
options.B: Collaborating
options.C: Competing
options.D: Smoothing

question: What is the primary purpose of evaluating directing effectiveness in a nursing unit?

options.A: Determining mandatory structural renovations for the building

options.C: Selecting new pharmaceutical vendors for the central store
options.D: Identifying performance gaps and guiding quality improvement

question: Which tool or framework is commonly utilized by nurse managers to test and implement changes resulting from directing evaluations?

options.A: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
options.B: Herzberg's Two-Factor Model
options.C: Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle
options.D: The Five Rights of Delegation

explanation: The PDSA cycle is a standard structured model used in healthcare quality improvement to test, study, and implement operational changes. [learn more](GST321_U1_T13#GST321_U1_T13_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of a nurse manager compared to a nurse leader?

options.A: Inspiring revolutionary changes in healthcare policy
options.B: Focusing exclusively on interpersonal staff charisma
options.C: Challenging the existing clinical status quo daily
options.D: Maintaining operational structure and efficiency

explanation: Management is fundamentally concerned with organizing resources, enforcing policies, and keeping daily ward operations running smoothly and predictably. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h1)

question: A staff nurse without an administrative title successfully rallies the ward team to adopt a new evidence-based wound care protocol by building enthusiasm and trust. What role is this nurse primarily demonstrating?

options.A: Leadership
options.B: Management
options.C: Administration
options.D: Supervision

explanation: Inspiring others and driving practice changes through influence and vision rather than formal title authority is the hallmark of leadership. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h1)

question: Which leadership theory posits that effective styles must change based on the maturity of the staff and the clinical environment?

options.A: Pure transactional leadership model
options.B: Situational and contingency theory
options.C: Innate behavioral trait theory
options.D: Great man leadership theory

explanation: Situational theories argue that there is no single best way to lead; instead, the approach must adapt to the specific context and readiness of the team. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h2)

question: A nurse manager relies heavily on an exchange system of performance bonuses, clear duty expectations, and corrective feedback for missed tasks. Which leadership style is being utilized?

options.A: Laissez-faire
options.B: Situational
options.C: Transactional
options.D: Transformational

question: When is an autocratic leadership style most appropriate in a clinical setting?

options.A: During a sudden emergency cardiac arrest resuscitation
options.B: During routine monthly nursing unit quality meetings
options.C: When orienting a newly graduated nurse to the ward
options.D: When designing a new flexible holiday roster for staff

explanation: Autocratic leadership is necessary during high-stakes emergencies where rapid, centralized command is required to coordinate life-saving actions. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h3)

question: A nurse manager who consistently allows highly autonomous intensive care nurses total freedom to manage their patient assignments without interference is practicing which style?

options.A: Laissez-faire
options.B: Autocratic
options.C: Transactional
options.D: Democratic

explanation: A laissez-faire leader provides minimal direction and grants complete operational freedom, which suits expert practitioners well. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h3)

question: What is considered the single greatest predictor of leadership success in healthcare professionals?

options.A: Length of time in the civil service
options.B: Emotional intelligence
options.C: Advanced chronological age
options.D: Strict authoritarian control

explanation: Emotional intelligence encompasses self-awareness, empathy, and social regulation, which are critical for navigating complex human relationships in healthcare. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h4)

question: A charge nurse openly acknowledges making a documentation error during shift handoff and takes steps to correct it immediately. Which essential leadership trait is primarily being demonstrated?

options.A: Autocratic command control
options.B: Laissez-faire delegation
options.C: Integrity and accountability
options.D: Transactional compliance

explanation: Owning up to mistakes rather than deflecting blame displays personal integrity and sets a professional standard of accountability for the team. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h4)

question: What is the core meaning of empowerment in a nursing leadership context?

options.A: Increasing the financial workload without adding compensation
options.B: Decentralizing power to give bedside nurses autonomy in decisions
options.C: Transferring all legal liability for errors entirely onto junior staff
options.D: Eliminating all management oversight across hospital departments

explanation: Empowerment means providing staff with the authority, resources, and trust to make meaningful decisions affecting their practice environment. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h5)

question: Which management practice best fosters intrinsic motivation among experienced clinical nurses?

options.A: Limiting access to continuing education seminars to save funds
options.B: Enforcing rigid, unyielding shift schedules without consultation
options.C: Threatening disciplinary queries for minor documentation delays
options.D: Recognizing individual clinical achievements and offering professional growth

explanation: Intrinsic motivation thrives when nurses feel valued, recognized for their contributions, and provided opportunities for career advancement. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h5)

question: Which conflict resolution strategy involves all parties working together openly to achieve a mutually satisfying win-win outcome?

options.A: Avoiding
options.B: Accommodating
options.C: Collaborating
options.D: Compromising

explanation: Collaboration focuses on deep problem-solving to ensure the core concerns of all parties are fully addressed and satisfied. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h6)

question: Two senior nurses disagree passionately about holiday shift scheduling, and both agree to each give up one preferred holiday to settle the dispute fairly. Which conflict style is being used?

options.A: Avoiding
options.B: Collaborating
options.C: Autocratic
options.D: Compromising

explanation: Compromising occurs when each individual makes concessions to find a mutually acceptable middle ground. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h6)

question: In Lewin’s change model, what is the primary purpose of the 'unfreezing' phase?

options.C: Evaluating the financial cost of purchasing new medical devices
options.D: Locking the final new protocol into permanent hospital policy

explanation: Unfreezing involves disrupting old routines and creating awareness of the need for change before introducing new behaviors. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h7)

question: A hospital ward has successfully adopted a new electronic health record system, and staff now use it instinctively as part of their normal daily routine. Which stage of change has been achieved?

options.A: Resisting
options.B: Unfreezing
options.C: Refreezing
options.D: Moving

explanation: Refreezing occurs when the newly introduced change is fully integrated and stabilized as the standard way of operating. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a core legal or ethical responsibility of a nurse leader?

options.A: Championing ethical patient advocacy across the healthcare facility
options.B: Protecting institutional whistleblowers who report clinical malpractice
options.C: Ensuring safe and appropriate delegation of clinical tasks to staff
options.D: Deliberately ignoring unsafe staffing shortages to save institutional funds

explanation: Ignoring unsafe staffing is a direct violation of professional, legal, and ethical obligations to maintain safe patient care environments. [learn more](GST321_U1_T14#GST321_U1_T14_h8)

question: A nurse manager discovers that a junior nurse has been improperly assigned to administer chemotherapy without specialized oncology certification. What primary leadership duty has been breached?

options.B: Transactional bonus distribution and financial auditing
options.C: Democratic consensus building for holiday rotations
options.D: Safe task delegation and scope of practice oversight

question: What is retained by the registered nurse when a task is delegated to another healthcare worker?

options.A: Ultimate accountability for the patient outcome
options.B: Direct legal liability for the worker's personal life
options.C: Exclusive authority to document in the medical record
options.D: Financial compensation for the delegated task

explanation: Even though the task is performed by someone else, the registered nurse keeps the legal and professional responsibility for the quality of care provided. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h1)

question: Why is proper delegation particularly vital in resource-constrained healthcare settings?

options.A: It shifts all legal blame completely to assistant staff
options.B: It eliminates the need for registered nurses on the ward
options.C: It reduces the total number of hospital admissions
options.D: It maximizes workforce efficiency to manage high patient volumes

explanation: When staff numbers are low, distributing routine tasks appropriately ensures all patients receive timely attention without overloading professionals. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h1)

question: Which of the Five Rights refers specifically to verifying that the patient's condition is stable?

options.A: Right Task
options.B: Right Direction
options.C: Right Circumstance
options.D: Right Person

explanation: Right Circumstance ensures that the clinical environment and patient stability warrant delegating a non-complex activity. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h2)

question: A nurse asks a ward orderly to administer an oral analgesic to a stable patient. Which right of delegation is primarily violated in this scenario?

options.A: Right Circumstance
options.B: Right Direction
options.C: Right Supervision
options.D: Right Task

explanation: Medication administration falls outside the scope of practice and job description of a ward orderly, making it the wrong task to delegate to them. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h2)

question: What is the primary responsibility of the delegatee upon receiving a task assignment?

options.A: Redelegating the task to a more junior colleague
options.B: Accepting only tasks within their training and scope
options.C: Evaluating the overall nursing care quality on the ward
options.D: Changing the patient care plan independently

explanation: Delegatees must recognize their own limitations and refuse assignments that exceed their legal and educational preparation. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h3)

question: Which core duty can a registered nurse NEVER transfer to an assistant personnel?

options.A: Transporting laboratory specimens to the hospital lab
options.B: Measuring routine vital signs on a stable patient
options.C: Assisting a patient with morning personal hygiene
options.D: Clinical assessment and professional judgment

explanation: Core nursing assessments and critical thinking decisions require professional licensure and cannot be delegated away. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h3)

question: What term describes a nurse who refuses to delegate tasks because they believe no one else can do them as well?

options.A: Maleficence
options.B: Insubordination
options.C: Overdelegation
options.D: Underdelegation

explanation: Underdelegation happens when the nurse inappropriately holds onto tasks due to a lack of trust or a desire to maintain total control. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h4)

question: What is a direct consequence of chronic overdelegation on a hospital ward?

options.A: Patient recovery rates increase due to rapid task execution
options.B: Registered nurses develop superior clinical assessment skills
options.C: The hospital completely eliminates the need for shift handovers
options.D: Assistant staff experience burnout and patient safety is compromised

explanation: Piling excessive duties onto subordinate workers overburdens them, leading to errors, missed care, and staff exhaustion. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h4)

question: Where does legal accountability remain after a registered nurse delegates a suitable task to a qualified assistant?

options.A: With the delegating registered nurse
options.B: With the ward cleaner on duty
options.C: With the hospital chief executive officer
options.D: With the patient receiving the care

explanation: The registered nurse retains ultimate accountability for choosing to delegate and for evaluating the overall outcome. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h5)

question: How should a nurse determine the appropriate level of supervision needed for a delegated task?

options.A: Based on the number of patients currently admitted to the hospital
options.B: Based entirely on the personal friendship between nurse and assistant
options.C: Based on the patient's clinical stability and the delegatee's competence
options.D: Based on the time of day the shift change occurs

explanation: Newer staff or unstable patients require much closer, direct oversight than experienced staff caring for stable individuals. [learn more](GST321_U1_T15#GST321_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the primary foundation of authority in a healthcare organization?

options.A: Official position within the organizational hierarchy
options.B: Personal charisma and interpersonal popularity
options.C: Advanced clinical certification in a specialty
options.D: Length of service within the nursing profession

explanation: Authority stems directly from the legitimate power granted by an official structural role rather than personal traits. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h1)

question: Why is formal authority essential for a clinical nurse manager?

options.A: It permits the enforcement of safety protocols and management of resources.
options.B: It eliminates the need for effective clinical communication.
options.C: It guarantees complete elimination of workplace conflict.
options.D: It replaces the requirement for professional nursing licensure.

explanation: Legitimate institutional backing gives managers the binding force required to direct work and maintain safety standards. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h1)

question: What type of authority is based primarily on codified rules, laws, and written job descriptions?

options.A: Traditional authority
options.B: Informal authority
options.C: Rational-legal authority
options.D: Charismatic authority

explanation: Rational-legal authority derives its legitimacy from explicit rules, statutory laws, and formal organizational structures. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h2)

question: How does expert authority differ fundamentally from formal administrative authority?

options.A: It applies only to administrative duties performed outside the hospital ward.
options.B: It is earned through specialized clinical knowledge rather than granted by an official title.
options.C: It is automatically assigned to every newly graduated registered nurse.
options.D: It carries the exclusive legal power to terminate employment contracts.

explanation: Expert authority relies on demonstrated competence and specialized skill that earns peer respect rather than a structural position. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h2)

question: What administrative term describes the absolute obligation to complete an assigned task and answer for the outcome?

options.A: Delegated control
options.B: Coercive power
options.C: Responsibility
options.D: Formal authority

explanation: Responsibility is the duty to perform tasks and accept the consequences of the resulting performance. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h3)

question: What happens when a nurse manager violates the principle of parity between authority and responsibility?

options.A: Informal power structures completely replace organizational hierarchy.
options.B: The need for formal job descriptions is permanently eliminated.
options.C: Clinical efficiency immediately improves through decentralized decision-making.
options.D: Staff experience frustration due to being held accountable for outcomes they cannot control.

explanation: When responsibility exceeds authority, staff face impossible expectations without the necessary tools or backing to succeed. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h3)

question: What element of delegation is retained by the professional nurse even after transferring task execution to a subordinate?

options.A: Coercive power
options.B: Accountability
options.C: Direct supervision
options.D: Hierarchical status

explanation: While task responsibility is transferred, the professional nurse retains ultimate accountability for the overall patient outcome. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h4)

question: A registered nurse is assigning duties on a busy surgical ward. Which consideration represents the core principle of safe delegation?

options.A: Matching the complexity of the nursing task with the competency level of the staff member
options.B: Ensuring that the delegating nurse performs no direct patient care during the shift
options.C: Assigning the most complex sterile procedures to the staff member who finishes first
options.D: Delegating all documentation tasks exclusively to newly employed auxiliary workers

explanation: Safe delegation requires evaluating staff competencies against specific task requirements to ensure patient safety. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h4)

question: Which factor is a common personal barrier preventing a nurse manager from delegating effectively?

options.A: Complete absence of organizational accountability frameworks
options.B: Too many written policies outlining clear delegation protocols
options.C: A tendency toward micro-management and reluctance to trust subordinates
options.D: An excess of available staff members on every hospital shift

explanation: Managers who struggle with trust and control often refuse to delegate, preferring to handle every task themselves. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h5)

question: How do rigid bureaucratic structures and unclear job descriptions negatively impact clinical delegation?

options.A: They automatically increase the clinical competency scores of junior auxiliary staff.
options.B: They guarantee complete parity between authority and responsibility for all workers.
options.C: They eliminate the need for any communication between nurses and physicians.
options.D: They create confusion regarding who is legally permitted to perform specific patient care tasks.

explanation: Unclear roles and rigid systems obscure legal boundaries, making safe and legal delegation difficult to execute. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of nursing regulatory councils establishing a legal scope of practice?

options.A: To determine the personal salary scales for individual nurse managers
options.B: To control the financial budgets of private healthcare institutions
options.C: To eliminate all forms of informal authority within hospital wards
options.D: To define the lawful boundaries of clinical interventions and protect the public

explanation: Regulatory bodies set scopes of practice to ensure public safety by establishing clear legal limits for nursing actions. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h6)

question: Why is peer review considered an important tool for maintaining professional control in nursing?

options.A: It grants junior nurses immediate administrative authority over senior physicians.
options.B: It evaluates clinical practice against professional standards using the insights of fellow practitioners.
options.C: It ensures that all staff members receive identical performance ratings annually.
options.D: It replaces the need for formal disciplinary hearings conducted by hospital management.

explanation: Peer review utilizes clinical colleagues to assess care quality, reinforcing professional accountability and continuous improvement. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h6)

question: What common systemic challenge significantly complicates the exercise of nursing authority in many Nigerian clinical settings?

options.A: Complete absence of any hierarchical administrative structure
options.B: An overabundance of advanced technological equipment on every ward
options.C: Total elimination of civil service regulations in public hospitals
options.D: Severe staff shortages and high patient-to-nurse ratios

explanation: Heavy workloads and staffing deficits strain managerial authority and make safe delegation and resource allocation difficult. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h7)

question: A ward manager in a busy Nigerian teaching hospital faces resistance to a new safety protocol due to cultural deference to seniority among staff. What is the most effective approach for the manager?

options.A: Combine formal authority with open dialogue and clear explanation of the safety rationale
options.B: Delegate all management responsibilities entirely to the youngest nurse on duty
options.C: Rely strictly on punitive civil service queries without discussing the underlying clinical issues
options.D: Abandon all formal protocols and let senior staff members decide ward routines informally

explanation: Balancing formal directives with respectful communication helps overcome cultural barriers while maintaining clinical safety standards. [learn more](GST321_U1_T16#GST321_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is the primary definition of professional accountability in nursing?

options.A: The legal right to delegate any medical task to junior staff
options.B: The requirement to work night shifts without direct supervision
options.C: The obligation to answer for one's own actions and omissions
options.D: The financial responsibility for hospital equipment maintenance

explanation: Accountability means taking ownership of your professional decisions and being answerable for the outcomes of your nursing care. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why is structured clinical supervision particularly critical in resource-constrained Nigerian healthcare environments?

options.A: It bridges theoretical learning with practice and protects patient safety
options.B: It removes all legal liability from the individual nurse
options.C: It replaces the need for formal nursing council registration
options.D: It guarantees automatic salary promotions after two years

explanation: In high-stress, low-resource settings, supervision ensures that standards remain high and novice nurses receive adequate guidance to protect patients from harm. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h1)

question: What is the primary difference between responsibility and accountability?

options.A: Responsibility applies only to doctors, while accountability applies only to nurses
options.B: Responsibility is legally binding, whereas accountability is purely voluntary
options.C: Accountability can be delegated entirely, but responsibility cannot
options.D: Responsibility is the obligation to perform a task, while accountability is being answerable for the outcome

explanation: You can delegate the performance of a task (responsibility), but the ultimate answerability for that choice remains with the person who delegated it (accountability). [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h2)

question: A nurse follows a doctor's written prescription without question, even though the dose is ten times the safe limit, and the patient suffers toxicity. Which statement best describes the nurse's accountability?

options.A: The nurse is only accountable if they administered the drug via the intravenous route
options.B: The nurse shares accountability because professional duty requires verifying unsafe orders
options.C: The nurse is solely accountable while the physician has complete immunity
options.D: The nurse bears no accountability because they were following a medical order

explanation: Nurses are independent professionals obligated to question and verify any order that appears unsafe or outside normal clinical parameters. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h2)

question: Which function of clinical supervision primarily deals with emotional support and managing burnout?

options.A: Legislative function
options.B: Normative function
options.C: Restorative function
options.D: Formative function

explanation: The restorative component focuses on the psychological well-being of the nurse, helping them cope with the emotional burdens of clinical practice. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h3)

question: When a supervisor reviews a nurse's documentation to ensure compliance with hospital policy and professional codes of conduct, which supervisory function is being utilized?

options.A: Restorative function
options.B: Normative function
options.C: Formative function
options.D: Therapeutic function

explanation: The normative function involves monitoring and maintaining professional standards, policies, and quality control. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h3)

question: What happens to accountability when a registered nurse delegates a task to a subordinate?

options.A: The registered nurse retains ultimate accountability for the overall outcome
options.B: Accountability is shared equally with the hospital administration
options.C: Accountability is eliminated entirely once the task is finished
options.D: Accountability transfers completely to the person who accepted the task

explanation: While the subordinate is responsible for performing the task correctly, the delegating nurse retains accountability for choosing to delegate it. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h4)

question: A staff nurse wants to assign vital sign collection for an unstable postoperative patient to a junior student nurse. Which of the Five Rights of Delegation is primarily violated in this scenario?

options.A: Right circumstance
options.B: Right task
options.C: Right supervision
options.D: Right direction

explanation: Delegating tasks involving unstable patients violates the right circumstance, as clinical instability requires higher-level professional assessment. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h4)

question: Which body is statutorily empowered to regulate nursing education and practice in Nigeria?

options.A: National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives
options.B: Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria
options.C: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.D: Federal Ministry of Health

explanation: The NMCN is the sole legal regulatory body responsible for setting standards, licensing, and disciplining nurses and midwives across Nigeria. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the primary consequence if a registered nurse is found guilty of gross professional negligence by the regulatory tribunal?

options.A: Financial compensation paid directly to the nursing union
options.B: Suspension or erasure of their name from the register
options.C: Mandatory attendance at a leadership seminar
options.D: A mandatory transfer to a rural health post

explanation: Severe professional misconduct or negligence leads to disciplinary actions by the NMCN tribunal, which can strip the practitioner of their license to practice. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is a major organizational barrier to effective clinical supervision in many busy hospitals?

options.A: An excess of highly trained supervisory personnel
options.B: Strict prohibition of mentorship by hospital bylaws
options.C: Complete absence of any clinical documentation
options.D: Chronic staff shortages and lack of protected time

explanation: When wards are understaffed, nurses are consumed by urgent clinical tasks, squeezing out dedicated time for supervision and mentorship. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h6)

question: How does a punitive, blame-oriented institutional culture negatively impact patient safety?

options.A: It forces nurses to work faster and accomplish more tasks per shift
options.B: It automatically increases the retention rate of senior staff
options.C: It drives errors and near-misses underground, preventing organizational learning
options.D: It eliminates the need for any written nursing care plans

explanation: When staff fear harsh punishment for admitting mistakes, they hide errors instead of reporting them, robbing the team of valuable opportunities to improve safety. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is the primary shift in focus when a healthcare facility adopts a modern safety culture regarding an error?

options.A: Shifting all financial penalties onto the hospital management
options.B: Ignoring minor errors to reduce paperwork
options.C: Punishing the entire shift team regardless of involvement
options.D: Moving from blame toward analyzing systemic root causes

explanation: A true safety culture looks beyond individual fault to identify and fix underlying system flaws that permitted the error to occur. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h7)

question: Which nursing activity directly contributes to continuous quality improvement on a clinical ward?

options.A: Refusing to participate in interprofessional team meetings
options.B: Participating in regular clinical audits and reflective practice
options.C: Avoiding documentation of near-misses to save time
options.D: Delegating all supervisory duties to non-nursing staff

explanation: Clinical audits and reflection allow nurses to systematically evaluate care practices, identify gaps, and implement targeted improvements. [learn more](GST321_U1_T17#GST321_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the primary definition of motivation in a professional setting?

options.A: The financial compensation provided at the end of the month
options.B: The physical strength required to complete heavy duties
options.C: The internal drive that energizes and directs behavior
options.D: The mandatory hospital policies enforced by administration

explanation: Motivation refers to the psychological forces that stimulate and sustain goal-directed actions in individuals. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h1)

question: Why is staff motivation particularly critical in resource-limited healthcare facilities?

options.A: It guarantees automatic promotion for all junior nursing personnel
options.B: It eliminates the need for any administrative oversight or scheduling
options.C: It helps sustain quality patient care and reduces burnout despite challenges
options.D: It directly compensates for a complete absence of hospital infrastructure

explanation: High morale and strong internal drive enable healthcare workers to maintain standards of care even when operating under difficult conditions. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h1)

question: According to Herzberg's two-factor theory, which of the following is classified as a hygiene factor?

options.A: Public recognition for a job well done
options.B: Personal growth opportunities
options.C: Increased professional responsibility
options.D: Job security and working conditions

explanation: Hygiene factors are extrinsic elements like salary and working conditions that prevent job dissatisfaction rather than actively motivating staff. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h2)

question: A staff nurse believes that working extra shifts will result in a promotion, and she values that promotion greatly. Which motivational theory best explains her drive to work harder?

options.A: Herzberg's two-factor theory
options.B: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
options.C: Classical conditioning theory
options.D: Vroom's expectancy theory

explanation: Expectancy theory focuses on the link between effort, performance, and the perceived value of the resulting reward. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h2)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of intrinsic motivation in nursing?

options.A: Finding personal fulfillment in a patient's successful recovery
options.B: Avoiding a query letter from the director of nursing
options.C: Receiving a monthly cash bonus for perfect attendance
options.D: Competing for the employee of the month award plaque

explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from internal satisfaction, such as the joy of helping others and personal pride in clinical competence. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h3)

question: What is a major limitation of relying exclusively on extrinsic motivators in a hospital unit?

options.A: They automatically cause severe physical exhaustion among staff
options.B: They completely fail to change short-term staff behavior
options.C: They are too inexpensive to be taken seriously by employees
options.D: They can diminish internal passion once the external reward is removed

explanation: Over-reliance on external rewards can undermine natural internal interest in the work itself, making long-term engagement dependent on constant rewards. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h3)

question: What leadership style focuses on inspiring subordinates through a shared vision and individualized support?

options.A: Autocratic management
options.B: Transactional oversight
options.C: Transformational leadership
options.D: Laissez-faire supervision

explanation: Transformational leaders inspire and motivate employees by connecting daily tasks to a broader purpose and supporting individual growth. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h4)

question: How does establishing psychological safety on a hospital ward impact staff motivation?

options.A: It removes all accountability for clinical medication mistakes
options.B: It ensures that nurses receive higher hazard allowances every month
options.C: It encourages open reporting of errors without fear, fostering trust
options.D: It allows nurses to skip mandatory continuing education units

explanation: When staff feel safe from unfair punishment, trust increases, leading to a healthier, more motivated, and proactive clinical team. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h4)

question: Which strategy directly addresses professional growth as a motivational tool?

options.A: Sponsoring attendance at clinical workshops and specialization training
options.B: Strictly enforcing disciplinary actions for minor documentation delays
options.C: Reducing the frequency of staff meetings across all hospital departments
options.D: Increasing the number of mandatory night shifts for junior staff

explanation: Supporting ongoing education and career advancement boosts morale by showing nurses that their professional future matters to the organization. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h5)

question: Why is fixing broken ward equipment an important part of maintaining nurse retention?

options.A: It guarantees that the hospital will receive international accreditation
options.B: It eliminates daily operational frustrations that contribute to burnout
options.C: It prevents patients from filing lawsuits against the hospital board
options.D: It replaces the need for financial salary increments entirely

explanation: Removing practical, environmental obstacles makes clinical work smoother and reduces the chronic frustration that drives nurses to leave the profession. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h5)

question: Which of the following is a direct method nurse managers use to assess staff sentiment?

options.A: Reviewing patient mortality statistics from the past decade
options.B: Auditing individual patient drug charts for calculation errors
options.C: Inspecting the physical cleanliness of the hospital kitchen
options.D: Anonymous climate surveys and feedback questionnaires

explanation: Surveys and questionnaires allow staff to express their feelings about workplace morale safely and anonymously. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h6)

question: What is the primary value of conducting thorough exit interviews with departing nurses?

options.A: To uncover root causes of dissatisfaction and improve retention strategies
options.B: To prevent the nurse from practicing in any other healthcare facility
options.C: To calculate the exact financial loss of onboarding a new employee
options.D: To finalize the immediate replacement schedule for the upcoming week

explanation: Exit interviews provide honest insights into why staff leave, helping management address systemic issues before other nurses resign. [learn more](GST321_U1_T18#GST321_U1_T18_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of the controlling function in healthcare management?

options.A: Designing the structural hierarchy of a nursing unit
options.B: Formulating long-term strategic plans for the institution
options.C: Monitoring activities to ensure goals and standards are met
options.D: Recruiting qualified personnel for vacant hospital wards

explanation: Controlling specifically involves tracking actual outcomes against set standards to ensure the organization stays on track. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h1)

question: Why is controlling considered a feedback loop rather than merely a punitive measure?

options.A: It focuses exclusively on reducing the salaries of clinical personnel
options.B: It eliminates the need for any future planning or organizing activities
options.C: It allows managers to punish staff members who make clinical errors
options.D: It provides actionable data to correct operational gaps and improve care

explanation: The primary intent of control systems is diagnostic and corrective, aiming to improve future performance rather than punish past mistakes. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h1)

question: What is the very first step in the management control process?

options.A: Taking corrective action
options.B: Establishing performance standards
options.C: Comparing results to benchmarks
options.D: Measuring actual performance

explanation: You cannot measure or control performance effectively without first defining what the acceptable standard or benchmark is. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h2)

question: A ward manager notices that patient wait times for wound dressings have doubled. According to the control process, what is the immediate next step after this discovery?

options.A: Compare the actual wait times against the established departmental benchmark
options.B: Rewrite the entire organizational mission statement for the hospital
options.C: Ignore the data because minor fluctuations happen in every ward
options.D: Instantly dismiss the nursing staff responsible for the dressing changes

explanation: Once performance is measured, the next step in the sequence is comparing those actual findings directly against the predetermined standard. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h2)

question: Which control system operates proactively before nursing care activities actually begin?

options.A: Concurrent control
options.B: Feedback control
options.C: Feedforward control
options.D: Retrospective control

explanation: Feedforward controls focus on preventing problems before they occur by screening inputs like personnel credentials and equipment readiness. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h3)

question: A nursing supervisor conducts a random audit of a nurse administering intravenous medication in real-time. What type of control is being demonstrated?

options.A: Feedforward control
options.B: Concurrent control
options.C: Financial control
options.D: Feedback control

explanation: Concurrent controls happen simultaneously as the work is being performed, allowing the manager to correct errors immediately at the bedside. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h3)

question: What type of indicator measures the final health status and recovery results of patients?

options.A: Process indicator
options.B: Outcome indicator
options.C: Structure indicator
options.D: Financial indicator

explanation: Outcome indicators focus on the end result of care provided, such as complication rates, recovery status, and patient mortality. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h4)

question: Which of the following represents a process indicator in a surgical ward?

options.A: Total number of functioning suction machines available in the emergency supply room
options.B: The ratio of registered nurses to patients on the morning duty shift
options.C: Percentage of surgical patients who received prophylactic antibiotics within the correct time window
options.D: Overall percentage of patients who report satisfaction with their hospital discharge instructions

explanation: Process indicators track whether specific clinical actions, steps, and protocols were correctly executed during care delivery. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h4)

question: What phenomenon occurs when clinical staff alter their normal behavior because they realize a manager is directly observing them?

options.A: Cognitive dissonance
options.B: The placebo phenomenon
options.C: The Hawthorne effect
options.D: Burnout syndrome

explanation: The Hawthorne effect describes how individuals modify their behavior simply in response to their awareness of being observed in a study or audit. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why is benchmarking an essential tool in healthcare management control?

options.A: It automatically punishes wards that fail to meet minimum budget allocations
options.B: It guarantees absolute immunity from legal malpractice lawsuits
options.C: It allows an institution to compare its metrics against recognized best practices
options.D: It replaces the need for direct observation and patient satisfaction surveys

explanation: Benchmarking gives managers an external frame of reference to evaluate how well their facility performs relative to industry leaders. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h5)

question: What type of variation stems from distinct, assignable errors rather than normal operational fluctuations?

options.A: Special-cause variation
options.B: Common-cause variation
options.C: Expected systemic variation
options.D: Random institutional variation

explanation: Special-cause variations are sporadic, identifiable disruptions that fall outside normal operating parameters and require specific intervention. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h6)

question: Why is reprimanding staff often an ineffective corrective action for systemic clinical errors?

options.A: It takes too much time away from actual patient care documentation
options.B: It violates international nursing labor laws across all jurisdictions
options.C: It fails to address the underlying root cause of the operational breakdown
options.D: It automatically increases the hospital's annual budgetary deficit

explanation: Effective corrective actions must analyze processes, equipment, or training gaps rather than blaming individuals for systemic flaws. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h6)

question: What management culture encourages staff to report near-misses and errors openly without immediate fear of reprisal?

options.A: A laissez-faire culture
options.B: A punitive culture
options.C: A just culture
options.D: A bureaucratic culture

explanation: A just culture balances individual accountability with organizational learning, encouraging transparent reporting of errors and near-misses. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a core dimension of healthcare quality in safety control frameworks?

options.A: Administrative profitability
options.B: Clinical effectiveness
options.C: Timeliness of care
options.D: Patient-centeredness

explanation: The recognized domains of healthcare quality focus on patient outcomes and care delivery parameters like safety, effectiveness, and timeliness, not institutional profit margins. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is a common reason clinical nursing staff resist management control systems?

options.A: They prefer having absolute control over hospital financial budgets
options.B: They believe control systems eliminate all forms of documentation
options.C: They are legally forbidden from participating in institutional audits
options.D: They perceive monitoring and audits as restrictive micromanagement

explanation: Staff often resist controls when they feel over-surveilled or disconnected from the purpose behind performance monitoring. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h8)

question: How can a nurse manager best overcome staff resistance to new performance control tools?

options.A: Involve frontline nurses in designing metrics and explain how data improves working conditions
options.B: Mandate strict compliance through immediate threats of suspension for minor errors
options.C: Keep all audit results completely secret from the nursing staff on the ward
options.D: Abandon all performance measurements until staff members request them voluntarily

explanation: Engagement and transparency build trust, helping staff see control tools as supportive mechanisms rather than punitive burdens. [learn more](GST321_U1_T19#GST321_U1_T19_h8)

question: What is the main difference between managing a healthcare facility and running a regular business?

options.A: Balancing financial viability with clinical outcomes
options.B: Maximizing shareholder dividends above all else
options.C: Focusing exclusively on building maintenance
options.D: Eliminating the need for nursing staff entirely

explanation: Unlike normal commercial businesses, healthcare managers always have to balance the cost of running the hospital with giving the best possible care to patients. You're doing great!

question: At what level does management happen in a hospital?

options.A: Only at the executive board room level
options.B: Exclusively within the hospital pharmacy department
options.C: At every level from charge nurse to director
options.D: Strictly during annual government audits

explanation: Management isn't just for bosses in suits! From frontline charge nurses managing the ward to senior directors, everyone plays a leadership role.

question: Why do nurse managers create a duty roster?

options.A: Ensuring 24-hour ward coverage without overworking staff
options.B: Determining the exact annual budget for the hospital
options.C: Punishing nurses who arrive late to work
options.D: Deciding which medications to purchase from vendors

explanation: A good duty roster makes sure patients are well cared for around the clock while keeping nurses fresh and preventing burnout.

question: A charge nurse expects more malaria cases during the rainy season and adds extra staff early. What management function is this?

options.A: Budgeting
options.B: Controlling
options.C: Planning
options.D: Delegating

explanation: Spotting future needs ahead of time and getting ready for them is the definition of planning. You're thinking like a true nurse leader!

question: What is the difference between the controlling and directing functions in nursing management?

options.A: Controlling focuses on hiring new staff, while directing deals exclusively with financial audits.
options.B: Controlling monitors performance and corrects errors, while directing guides and motivates staff.
options.C: Controlling happens before planning, while directing happens after discharge.
options.D: Controlling is done only by doctors, while directing is done only by auxiliary nurses.

explanation: Think of directing as leading and encouraging your team day-to-day, while controlling is checking that standards are met and fixing things when they go wrong.

question: Which of these is a clear example of the controlling function in a hospital ward?

options.A: Investigating why a medication error occurred and retraining the staff
options.B: Writing a motivational speech for the morning handover meeting
options.C: Purchasing new beds for an upcoming private ward extension
options.D: Designing a colourful poster about hand hygiene for the lobby

explanation: Finding out why a mistake happened and taking steps to fix it falls right under controlling, keeping patient safety standards high.

question: Which management theory focuses the most on efficiency, timing tasks, and standard work routines?

options.A: Human Relations Theory
options.B: Democratic Leadership Theory
options.C: Chaos Management Theory
options.D: Scientific Management

explanation: Scientific management looks closely at how tasks are done to cut out wasted time and make every action as efficient as possible.

question: A nurse manager holds a team meeting just to check on staff morale and listen to personal concerns. Which theory supports this?

options.A: Classical Command Theory
options.B: Scientific Management
options.C: Human Relations Theory
options.D: Bureaucratic Theory

explanation: The human relations approach reminds us that workers have social and emotional needs, and keeping morale high makes a huge difference.

question: During a sudden emergency on the ward, the charge nurse gives quick, direct orders without debating. What leadership style is this?

options.A: Democratic
options.B: Laissez-Faire
options.C: Autocratic
options.D: Transformational

explanation: In an emergency, there's no time for a committee meeting! An autocratic style gives fast, clear direction when every second counts.

question: Which of these describes a democratic leadership style in healthcare?

options.A: Making all choices independently without consulting any staff members
options.B: Involving team members in discussions and valuing their input on decisions
options.C: Leaving the ward completely unattended to let nurses work on their own
options.D: Punishing staff members publicly for minor documentation errors

explanation: Democratic leaders bring the team together, listen to everyone's ideas, and make choices collaboratively.

question: What is the very first step when solving a problem?

options.A: Identifying and clearly defining the problem
options.B: Implementing a quick temporary fix immediately
options.C: Writing a formal report for the hospital board
options.D: Blaming the staff member who made the error

explanation: You can't fix an issue until you truly understand what is going wrong. Pinpoint the real problem first!

question: What is the main difference between decision-making and problem-solving?

options.A: Decision-making is choosing one option among alternatives, while problem-solving involves finding the root cause of an issue.
options.B: Decision-making requires no data collection, while problem-solving requires a government health budget.
options.C: Decision-making is a slow academic exercise, whereas problem-solving is always completed in seconds.
options.D: Decision-making is only done by physicians, while problem-solving is restricted to administrative managers.

explanation: Decision-making means picking a choice from a few options, while problem-solving is the bigger journey of tracking down and fixing an underlying issue.

question: Which type of budget takes care of daily running costs like medical supplies and generator fuel?

options.A: Emergency surplus budget
options.B: Capital budget
options.C: Operational budget
options.D: Personal investment budget

explanation: The operational budget keeps the lights on and the supplies stocked for everyday patient care.

question: Why is resource management often tough in public Nigerian healthcare facilities?

options.A: Hospitals have excess funds that are difficult to spend before the year ends
options.B: There are too many nurses available for every single hospital bed
options.C: Financial resources and medical supplies are often limited compared to the patient load
options.D: Patients refuse to use any medications provided by the government

explanation: When funds and supplies are tight compared to the heavy number of patients, nurse managers have to be very smart about prioritizing.

question: What is the main goal of a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) after something goes wrong in the hospital?

options.A: Calculating the financial cost of lost equipment
options.B: Finding a junior nurse to blame and dismissing them immediately
options.C: Hiding the incident from the hospital management board
options.D: Discovering underlying system flaws that allowed the error to happen

explanation: RCA doesn't look for someone to point a finger at; it digs deep into the system to fix broken processes so it never happens again.

question: What does a 'just culture' mean for patient safety in a hospital?

options.A: A strict legal system where every single mistake results in immediate court prosecution
options.B: An administrative rule that hides medical errors from patients and their families
options.C: A policy that protects senior doctors from ever facing disciplinary action
options.D: A work environment where staff can report errors openly to fix system flaws without unfair punishment

explanation: In a just culture, nurses feel safe speaking up about mistakes without fear, helping the whole team learn and protect patients better.

question: What is the final phase of the classical administrative process in nursing management?

options.A: Organizing
options.B: Controlling
options.C: Planning
options.D: Directing

explanation: Controlling follows planning, organizing, and directing in the management cycle, focusing on measuring performance against benchmarks. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why are established standards essential for the controlling phase of management?

options.A: They replace the need for initial planning and policy creation
options.B: They serve as objective yardsticks to measure actual performance
options.C: They automatically increase hospital funding from the government
options.D: They eliminate the need for hiring additional nurse managers

explanation: Without predetermined criteria, nurse managers cannot objectively evaluate whether clinical work meets required quality and safety levels. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h1)

question: What do performance standards primarily describe in a clinical setting?

options.A: The acceptable level of performance or behavior required
options.B: The specific brand of medical supplies to purchase
options.C: The architectural layout of a standard hospital ward
options.D: The exact monthly salary scale for nursing personnel

explanation: Performance standards define the expected quality of care and professional behavior nurses must deliver. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h2)

question: How do well-defined performance standards protect both patients and nurses?

options.A: By removing the need for continuous professional education
options.B: By providing clear legal benchmarks and reducing practice ambiguity
options.C: By transferring all liability directly to the hospital board
options.D: By guaranteeing immunity from all forms of civil litigation

explanation: Clear standards establish what constitutes safe practice, which protects patients from harm and gives nurses clear operational boundaries. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h2)

question: Which of the following is an example of a quantitative standard?

options.A: Patient satisfaction level
options.B: Compassionate bedside manner
options.C: Therapeutic communication
options.D: Nurse-to-patient ratio

explanation: Quantitative standards involve measurable numbers and counts, such as specific staffing ratios or timing frequencies. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h3)

question: A nurse manager evaluating the empathy and patient comfort conveyed during wound dressing changes is assessing what type of standard?

options.A: Financial standard
options.B: Qualitative standard
options.C: Quantitative standard
options.D: Structural standard

explanation: Qualitative standards focus on the human experience, clinical excellence, and intangible aspects of care like empathy. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h3)

question: What is a key characteristic of an effective nursing performance standard?

options.A: It must be realistic and achievable given available resources
options.B: It must focus exclusively on hospital financial profits
options.C: It should be kept secret from junior nursing staff
options.D: It needs to change completely during every shift change

explanation: Standards must be practical and attainable within the realities of the clinical environment to be useful. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h4)

question: A hospital drafts a standard stating that 'all nurses must eliminate hospital-acquired infections completely by next week.' Which principle of effective standards does this violate?

options.A: Being time-bound and structured
options.B: Being aligned with regulatory bodies
options.C: Being focused on qualitative metrics
options.D: Being achievable and realistic

explanation: Completely eliminating infections within a week is an unrealistic expectation that ignores complex clinical variables. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h4)

question: What is the initial step when establishing a new clinical standard?

options.A: Drafting immediate disciplinary policies
options.B: Punishing staff who fail previous audits
options.C: Purchasing expensive foreign equipment
options.D: Reviewing current evidence and research findings

explanation: Evidence-based practice forms the baseline for creating valid and scientifically sound clinical standards. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h5)

question: Why is pilot testing a new nursing standard on a single ward recommended before a full hospital rollout?

options.A: To identify and correct unforeseen operational hurdles early
options.B: To reduce the total number of patients admitted to the hospital
options.C: To ensure only senior nurses ever have to practice using it
options.D: To hide the new policies from strict government regulators

explanation: Pilot testing allows management to spot practical difficulties and refine the standard before wider implementation. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h5)

question: Which body is primarily responsible for establishing the scope of nursing practice and professional ethics in Nigeria?

options.A: Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs
options.B: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.C: National Association of Resident Doctors
options.D: World Health Organization Africa Office

explanation: The NMCN is the statutory body charged with regulating nursing education and practice standards in Nigeria. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h6)

question: When a hospital creates its internal clinical standards, what must nurse managers ensure regarding national regulatory bodies?

options.A: Internal protocols must align with and not contradict national guidelines
options.B: Regulatory bodies must personally approve every single ward duty roster
options.C: Internal standards must replace national council examinations
options.D: National guidelines can be completely ignored if hospital profit is high

explanation: Hospital standards must always comply with the minimum legal and professional requirements set by national regulatory authorities. [learn more](GST321_U1_T20#GST321_U1_T20_h6)

question: Which of the following is a common operational barrier to implementing standards in resource-constrained Nigerian health facilities?
